title: A contact path for an accounting firm
metaTitle: Accounting firm contact page that books a call
excerpt: An accounting firm contact page should say what happens next, how fast you reply, and what to have ready. Ten fields lose a founder who was ready to book.
alt: A clothing shop interior with folded shirts, hanging jackets, shelves, and pendant lights, a room where the offer is laid out in the open the way a contact page should be.
caption: Shirts, jackets, and shelves under ordinary lights, the stock easy to see. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an accounting contact page explain first?
faqs.answer: Explain what happens after they book, who they will meet, and how fast a person confirms on a normal week. Say that the call is a fit check, not a finished return, and that they are not engaged yet. A founder can plan around a true sentence.

faqs.question: What should a founder have ready?
faqs.answer: The kind of company, the entity if they know it, how the records are kept, and the question or date that prompted the search. Last year's return can wait until the confirmation email if uploading on a phone is likely to stall them. Not sure is an acceptable answer.

faqs.question: Why do long contact forms backfire?
faqs.answer: Each extra field is a pause, and people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds when the page stops being clear. A ten-field form feels like an application. Collect company numbers and long histories after a human has said the work fits.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An accounting firm contact page should tell a founder who needs a calm expert what happens after they reach out, how fast a person replies, and what to have ready. The action is to book a call. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them after they have already decided you might be the right kind of firm.

They are often slightly embarrassed about the state of the books. The page should not add theater. It should make the next step small and predictable. Nielsen Norman Group's research is a fair clock. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and they read only about a quarter of the text on pages they open. Spend that quarter on the promise of a reply, not on a skyline and the word excellence.

## What happens after they book

Write the sequence in a few sentences above the form or the calendar.

They book a call, or they send a note if you are not using a calendar. A named person, or a named role, reads it. You reply with whether this kind of company and this kind of question are ones you take, and you confirm the time. The call is a fit check. It is not a completed return, and it does not mean they have engaged you for the year.

If a coordinator schedules and an accountant does the call, say both. Founders forgive a clear path. They do not forgive discovering on the day that they prepared a year's story for someone who cannot help.

Say what you will not do before the call. You will not rebuild the ledger from the booking email. You will not guess a tax position from a sentence. That limit is part of being careful, and it lowers the temperature. Calm includes refusing to pretend the email was an engagement.

If the calendar is live, say whether the slot is confirmed or held until you accept it. If you accept manually, say how fast that acceptance comes. A founder who blocks an hour and hears nothing will not describe you as calm, whatever the photography says.

## How fast, in a sentence you can keep

Publish a speed you already keep. "We confirm bookings the same business day when the request arrives before three, otherwise the next business day" is a real sentence if it is true. "We respond promptly" is a mood. A founder timing a raise or a filing date cannot plan on a mood.

Build the promise around business days if you do not work Sundays. Update the line when the office is closed for a known stretch. An auto-reply that contradicts the website is a small crack in trust, and Google's helpful-content guidance treats trust as the core of experience and expertise on topics that affect financial stability. This page is that kind of page. A slower true sentence beats a fast false one.

The confirmation should repeat the speed and the address they can use if the form fails. "You will get a note at the email you entered by the next business day." Include what the note will decide: fit, the shape of the first phase, and what to send next. Do not pivot into a newsletter.

## What to have ready

A short list beside the booking makes the call useful and stops people abandoning the form to go hunting.

Four things are enough for most founders.

- The kind of company. Studio, clinic, shop, product company, trade. Rough size in people, if that changes who you take.
- The entity type, as far as they know. Company, sole trader, trust, partnership. "Not sure" is an acceptable answer.
- How the records are kept. The name of the ledger, a folder of exports, or "mostly in my head." Shame does not belong in the instructions. Accuracy does.
- The question they want answered, and any date attached to it. A notice, a lender, a year-end, a co-founder who wants a number.

Last year's return helps if they can find it. Do not require the upload before they may book. Phone uploads are where founders stall. They can bring the file to the call or reply to your confirmation with it.

Do not ask for a marketing source, a budget range, their date of birth, or "tell us your vision" before the fit check. Those serve the firm. The founder is trying to learn whether you are the person. The story can happen on the call, where someone can be kind about a messy year.

If you need a conflict-style check, such as whether you already act for their co-founder or their competitor, ask for the other name only when it matters. A corporate family tree can wait.

## The form, if you use one

Some firms book straight onto a calendar. Some ask for a note first. Either can be calm. A pile of fields cannot.

Each field needs a visible label, not only a placeholder that disappears. W3C's WCAG overview describes a standard that applies to forms and to mobile, built around pages that are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A vanishing label fails the first of those, and it fails a founder who gets interrupted and returns.

Mark the few required fields. Let the deadline be "none" or "not sure." Let the file be optional. The button says "Book a call," the same words as the rest of the site. "Submit" is a database talking.

Show errors beside the field in text. Do not clear what they typed. Do not rely on a red border alone. On a phone, the button has to remain reachable when the keyboard is open. Test that with a thumb.

After a successful send, repeat the sequence. Do not drop them on a generic thank-you that sells a different service or a download. The next thing they need is the promise you just made, restated, plus the email address as text they can copy.

## Ten fields is how a ready founder leaves

Count the inputs. If you are near ten, you are screening them out.

Extras that feel tidy inside the firm and heavy outside it: legal name and trading name and company number, postal address, preferred office, referral source, a dropdown of services that do not match your headings, a second phone, a captcha that fails, a terms PDF that must be opened, and a text area titled "describe your business in detail."

Each extra is a chance to go find a number they do not have in the hallway. The first seconds are when people decide to stay. A form that looks like a loan application fails that test even if the headline was human.

Cut back to the call. Collect the formal facts after a person has said the work fits, in the engagement that follows. The website does not have to be the engagement letter.

If a regulator expects a specific warning, put it in readable type near the button, short enough to finish. A wall of disclaimer above the only action teaches them the firm is more interested in cover than in the question they brought.

## The rest of the page

Under or beside the booking, keep this order. The sequence and the speed. What to have ready. The hours. Who they will meet, with a link to that person. A link back to the kinds of companies you serve, for someone who landed here from search and has not seen the homepage.

An address matters when visits happen. Many accounting relationships do not need a visit. Do not let a map of the car park push the booking below the first phone screen. Text address beats a pin when they are copying it, and it is more reliable for someone who cannot use the map.

Email should be a real address a person reads, printed as text, for the day the form fails. A contact page with no escape hatch except the form is fragile. Phone, if you list it, needs hours and a purpose. A voicemail nobody checks is not a backup plan.

Skip the skyline on this page. They are trying to hand you a question. A city does not take the question. A person does.

## Before you publish

Book a call with yourself from a phone. Confirm the note that arrives contains the company type, the ledger, and a return address. Confirm the sender saw the promise, not a blank state. Reply in the way the page claims, and see if the speed is true.

Ask a colleague to book as a studio founder with a year that went quiet. Watch where they hesitate. If they apologize for not attaching a file you marked optional, the layout still makes it feel mandatory. If they cannot tell who they will meet, the sequence is missing a name.

Then read the page for costume. Excellence in the heading, a glass building, a chatbot that implies an accountant is typing. Remove them. The booking is the point.

Once the path is short, the rest of the site is often too long. Read [what to leave off the site](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-an-accounting-firm) before you add a banner above the form.

When you want to see how a specific offer is presented without the extra costume, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The contact page should be the simplest page you ship.
